newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean banks set Jinro bail-out at $90 million.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean banks set Jinro bail-out at $90 million.

text.p: South Korean banks on Monday agreed to a 80.4 billion won ($90 million) emergency loan to the troubled Jinro Group to avoid what would be the third major corporate failure this year.
An official of a banks committee told reporters after the meeting the emergency loans would be disbursed "as soon as possible". Jinro originally sought 500 billion won in emergency loans.

But the official of the Commercial Bank of Korea, Jinro's main creditor, added that group chairman Chang Jin-ho would first be required to issue a letter authorising banks to dispose of his family's shares of group affiliates.
It was not clear whether Chang had already agreed to give up his family's ownership and management rights in the group.
An earlier decision by the bank committee to defer debt payments for the group's six core affiliates would be in effect until July 21, the committee official said.
At the end of 1996, those six firms accounted for 80.7 percent of the group's total sales turnover and 90 percent of total assets, according to data released by the Commercial Bank.
Chang told reporters after the committee meeting he would like to make one or two substitutions to the six companies slated for rescue, but he did not elaborate. The group has 24 affiliates.
The committee official said Jinro Ltd, the group's flagship and the nation's largest and oldest distilled liquor maker, would get 25.1 billion won of the emergency loans.

Four others and their shares are: Jinro Mass-Merchandising Inc, 32.3 billion won; Jinro Construction Co, 13.7 billion won; Jinro Industries Co, 5.0 billion won; and Jinro General Foods Co, 4.3 billion won.
The fifth, Jinro-Coors Brewing Co, is expected to receive a cash infusion from its partner or a third party.
Jinro, the 19th-largest business group, buckled this month under 3.2 trillion won in debt, mostly a result of reckless expansion.
The group said it would sell part of its property and affiliates to raise about 1.2 trillion won by the end of 1998 to repay debts estimated at 3.2 trillion won.
Earlier on Monday, South Korea's 30 merchant banks said they would join the committee after commercial banks accepted their demand to exempt them from offering additional credit.
Participation of the merchant banks removed a major obstacle to rescuing the stricken group.

With the country still reeling from the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March, the government last week said it would set up a 1.5 trillion won fund to buy, repackage and sell banks' bad debts.
Analysts said the government worried that a third high-profile bankruptcy would reveal the weakness of the country's banking system in the run-up to December's presidential election.

"I think the Korean authorities are actually more worried about what happens in the commercial banking system than they are with one manufacturing company," said Graham Courtney, director of Asian economics at SBC Warburg in Tokyo.
